families.s: HSE management systems for maintenance, inspection and testing
families.t: resources, staffing, backlogs, policy, organising, planning, measurement, audit, review and senior management
f: Maintenance, inspection and testing are key activities, especially in major-hazard industries.
Performance can be assessed through outputs such as maintenance backlogs.
The management process should also be assessed rather than relying only on output measures.
HSE identifies policy, organising, planning, measuring, auditing and review as relevant management elements.
Organisations should confirm that adequate resources are available for necessary maintenance, inspection and testing.
Organisations should confirm that adequate staff are available for these activities.
Senior managers should understand the consequences of failing to provide required resources.
MIT management should address planning, execution, records, backlog control, verification and improvement.
families.g: Resources, staffing, backlogs, policy, organising, planning, measurement, audit, review and senior management guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE prevention of human error during maintenance
families.t: slips, omissions, reassembly, replacement parts, recommissioning, safety features, set points, tools and independent verification
f: Experienced, trained and motivated technicians can still make slips and omissions.
Maintenance errors can initiate major accidents and injure maintenance personnel.
Maintenance quality depends heavily on human activity.
Maintenance actions and decisions should not leave equipment or systems unsafe.
Common failures include incorrect reassembly and use of the wrong replacement specification.
Other failures include omitted steps, recommissioning errors and disconnected safety features.
Incorrect instrument set points or tools left inside equipment can create serious hazards.
Task design, procedures, checking, supervision and formal return to service should reduce maintenance error.

families.s: HSE intelligent-customer capability for contracted safety work
families.t: client knowledge, hazard proportionality, core competence, corporate memory, contractor qualification, methodology, limitations and regulatory accountability
f: Intelligent-customer capability is the organisation's ability to understand the product or service being supplied.
It is particularly important when organisations contract out safety-related activities.
The required capability should be proportionate to the hazard and size of the organisation.
Core competence and corporate memory should be retained.
Staff turnover, succession planning, competence, communication and lessons learned affect this capability.
Clients should be able to judge whether contractors are suitably qualified.
Clients should understand and challenge the methodology used for contracted safety analyses.
The organisation should understand limitations and implications and remain able to present and defend its safety case.

families.s: HSE organisational controls for outsourcing and contractorisation
families.t: outsourcing, restructuring, client responsibility, selection, coordination, induction, supervision, competence and corporate memory
f: Contractorisation can result from downsizing, restructuring or initiatives to replace or supplement company staff.
Contracted services may be performed on-site or away from the client's premises.
The client must retain knowledge of the supplied product or service.
The client remains responsible for managing safe operations.
Selection should consider resources, equipment, knowledge and experience.
Coordination should define responsibilities, timing and methods across clients, contractors and subcontractors.
Induction should cover site rules, procedures, hazards and emergency arrangements.
Supervision, contractor competence and retention of corporate memory are essential controls.

families.s: HSE management of fatigue and shift-working risks
families.t: working time, shift patterns, rest, sleep loss, body clock, workload, reaction time, memory, awareness and organisational control
f: Poor shift design and long hours without sufficient rest and recovery can cause fatigue, accidents, injury and ill health.
Fatigue is a decline in mental or physical performance linked to prolonged exertion, sleep loss or body-clock disruption.
Complex, machine-paced or monotonous work can increase fatigue.
Fatigue can slow reactions and reduce information processing.
It can cause memory lapses, absent-mindedness and reduced awareness.
Fatigue can reduce attention and coordination and lead people to underestimate risk.
Fatigue has been identified as a root cause in major accidents.
Employers should manage working hours, shift patterns, workload, breaks and recovery rather than rely only on individual coping.
